Each box should do something - run a function in one of the files in the SRC directory within the directory where we're storing the FSM structural files. It could be a function in a library (only public functions of course) like in C, or it could be a bash script or something. We want to be agnostic to what the user wants to do. We should also be able to create data files that include things like structs and such. For now, let's build for lua only functionality - storing tables in data files with json using dkjson, and doing all of the control flow with lua. The web application should simply be a UI to manipulate the local files, but we might later implement an HTTP server that lets a user control it remotely or something like that - open to discussion. We want simple control flow, with if/then/else, for loops, and anything else that seems reasonable. ### feedback_cross_language_pitfalls.md

```markdown
---
name: Cross-language design pitfalls
description: Three approaches the user rejected when designing SoraMech's cross-language wire format
type: feedback
originSessionId: e9ed70c7-2b63-425c-987c-6431040bedfb
---
When designing anything that touches the cross-language data path, avoid these three shapes — the user pushed back on each and the rejections are load-bearing for the architecture.

**1. Don't propose runtime "handles" that route operations back to the originating spec.**

**Why:** Real library functions in the wild (qsort, libcurl, anything from libc) expect actual native values — a real `int (*)(int,int)` function pointer, a real `char *` — not a SoraMech-issued id string. They can't be modified to participate in our runtime's routing scheme. The wire must carry data the destination spec can fully reconstruct into a native value, not opaque tokens.

**How to apply:** When a value seems hard to serialize (function pointers, coroutines, opaque pointers), decompose to data primitives (address + signature, bytecode + upvalues, ptr + length). If the destination needs a callable, the destination spec synthesizes one at reconstruction time (libffi trampoline for C, `ffi.cast` for LuaJIT). The "phone home" callback that the trampoline performs internally is fine — it's an artifact of the destination spec's reconstruction, not exposed in the wire format. What's forbidden is a wire primitive that says "operations on this value cross back to the source."

**2. Don't propose pair-wise language conversion paths (lua→c, c→lua, etc.).**

**Why:** N languages means N² conversion paths, which means adding a new language breaks the existing ones. The wire must use a language-agnostic intermediate (JSON) and every spec must implement only the two pair-symmetric callbacks (`to_json`, `from_json`). New language = implement those two functions, nothing else touches.

**How to apply:** Never write code that names two specific languages in a conversion context. Specs only ever see JSON on the wire. If a JSON primitive needs an extension (like `$function_pointer`), it lives in the universal JSON contract, not as a lua-spec-specific or c-spec-specific concept.

**3. Don't propose per-function annotations for type ambiguities (lengths, discriminators, callback signatures).**

**Why:** The user pointed out that "discriminator" is a vocab word the system has no general way to ask about. We can't prompt "which param is the length?" because that pairing convention lives in the function's English documentation, not its types. Asking the user to write annotations means asking them to know specialized vocabulary they didn't sign up for.

**How to apply:** When a function signature has ambiguous types (`char *` with no length, `union` with no tag, `void *` with no signature), expose each parameter as a separate input slot on the box. The user wires the slots according to the function's documentation — `p` from one source, `n` from another. The system never infers pairings; the user expresses them by wiring. If the destination needs a length and no length wire is provided, the wire compile fails with a plain-English fix-it message ("destination needs length, source provides only a pointer — wire a length input here").

**Common thread:** all three rejections are the same principle in different clothes — **SoraMech bends to the language, not the other way around.** Users write idiomatic code in their language. Libraries are used as-is. Specs are self-contained and pair-symmetric. The system stays out of the user's vocabulary.

```

### project_cross_language_wire.md

```markdown
---
name: Cross-language wire format
description: Dual-ring slot per port (native ring + JSON ring + ordering ring). JSON only at language borders. Per-edge classification at graph load; per-cell precision at runtime.
type: project
originSessionId: 5670858b-274f-49c4-89b8-a4b83ce33d7c
---
Design corrected 2026-05-21 — replaces the older "JSON always" framing.

**Each input slot is a dual-ring buffer.** Per port: one `ring_native` (consumer-language native bytes), one `ring_json` (JSON bytes from cross-language producers), and one `ring_order` of `(which_ring, idx)` tuples in arrival order. Allocate `ring_json` and `ring_order` lazily — same-language-only ports pay nothing for them.

**Push selects ring by per-edge bit.** Producer's spec writes native bytes to `ring_native` if `output_edge_native[j]` is true; otherwise calls `native_to_json` and writes to `ring_json`. Either way, pushes a `(which_ring, idx)` tuple to `ring_order`.

**Pop reads ordering ring first.** Dispatch pops `ring_order`, gets `(which_ring, idx)`, then pops the indicated cell. The consumer's spec receives `(input_data[i], input_native[i])` per input port and dispatches per flag — decode native or decode JSON.

**Why dual-ring instead of per-port classification.** Per-port (slot is all-JSON if any fan-in is cross-lang) is the pessimistic approximation — same-language values eat JSON cost on mixed-fan-in ports. Dual-ring is precise per cell: a port fed by one Lua box and one C box keeps the Lua cells native and JSON-encodes only the C-sourced cells.

**Why JSON for the cross-language ring (not pair-wise paths, not type-annotated raw bytes).** JSON's structure is self-describing — every language has a natural mapping for object/array/number/string/bool/null. Adding language K means K's spec implements its own `native_to_json` and `json_to_native`. N spec-pairs, not N² language-pair paths. The native ring's format is each spec's private choice — Lua may pick msgpack or `cjson.encode` or a custom binary form; C uses `memcpy` of the wrapper struct; Bash uses strings.

**Sentinel primitives for non-JSON-mappable values.** `$ref` (pointer + length into the large-value heap), `$function_pointer`, `$lang_opaque` ("these bytes are language-X-internal"). Carried inside the JSON ring as object-shaped sentinels. Cross-language receivers that can't reconstruct fail at wire compile.

**`$function_pointer` reconstruction — wrapper binary + persistent subprocess (issue 318, amended 2026-05-22).** Earlier design had the consumer's spec FFI-cast the raw process-local address. Rejected: FFI is language-pair-specific, biases SoraMech toward the Lua↔C corner, breaks the N-not-N² rule. Replacement: at map-compile time the compiler asks the *producing* spec to compile the referenced function + its enumerable dependencies into a standalone wrapper binary on disk that speaks a small line protocol on stdio. The consumer spec spawns one persistent subprocess per `$function_pointer` it receives and talks to it over the same socket-like channel used for any out-of-process spec. Every language pays the same price; new languages only implement "compile a function to a wrapper binary" — no pair-wise FFI knowledge required.

**Spec `invoke` signature change.** Collapses `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` into one `invoke` with per-input/per-output flags: `int invoke(handle, ..., const int *input_native, int n_inputs, int output_native, void *out_buf, ...)`. The spec dispatches per input internally. This is the contract change that unblocks 306/307's typed marshalling.

**Two compile-time layers stack:**
- **Per-edge classification (issue 312, this design)** — graph loader computes `input_edge_native[]` and `output_edge_native[]` on each box; dispatch routes pushes accordingly. This issue is the wire-format design.
- **Same-language source merge (issue 313, research / blocked)** — concatenate every same-language box's source into one translation unit per language. Boxes still run as separate thread-pool tasks; what 313 thins is the spec invocation overhead inside the merged region (direct call into the worker's `lua_State` instead of dlsym + marshal + bridge). The dual-ring slot machinery does NOT collapse — tasks still need slots to wait for sibling inputs. 313 makes the ring cells cheaper to read/write; it doesn't remove them.

**Three rejected design shapes** (kept here so they don't get reinvented):
1. **Handles back-routing to the owning spec** — library functions in the wild can't be modified to use SoraMech-shaped handles. Rejected.
2. **Pair-wise language paths** — every new language would have to grow N-1 translation paths against existing languages. Rejected. The dual-ring's "two rings per slot" is the dimension-cap that prevents this.
3. **Per-function discriminator / length annotations on the wire** — the system has no universal vocabulary to ask "is param 2 the length?" Rejected; the user expresses these by wiring two separate input slots.

**How to apply:** When discussing wire format, slot store shape, dispatch routing, or spec callbacks: think dual-ring (native, JSON, ordering) per slot, per-edge classification at push time, per-cell tag at pop time, JSON-only-at-borders, language-private native bytes everywhere else.

```

### project_custom_translation_specs.md

```markdown
---
name: Custom translation specs per port
description: Users can override the default native/JSON wire path on any input port for any reason — a knob in the wire format vocabulary (issue 246)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**Per-port custom translation specs** let the user intervene at a specific input port and replace the default dual-ring decode path with user-written code. The override applies to that one port; the rest of the graph uses the default native-or-JSON path from issue 312.

**Motivating cases (any reason qualifies, not just cross-language):**
- Cross-language ambiguity the default specs can't infer: a C++ class with methods landing at a C box (drop methods? expose as fn pointers? restructure?), a `void *` carrying a libcurl handle, a union whose discriminator is on a separate wire.
- Same-language reshape: massaging a value into a different shape on its way in (rename fields, drop a layer, project a subset) without adding a transform box on the canvas.
- Validation / coercion: clamp a number, enforce a schema, fail loudly on unexpected shapes.

**How it composes with the dual-ring design:**
- The custom spec runs at *pop* time on the consumer side, after the ordering ring has been consulted and the cell has been read from the appropriate ring. The user's code receives the decoded value (native or JSON-decoded) and produces whatever the consumer's `invoke` will see.
- A port with a custom translation gets its own wire color in the editor (issue 245) — visible signal that this port doesn't use the default path.

**Why:** The default native/JSON contract covers the cases JSON's structure handles cleanly. Everything outside that needs a user escape hatch — *and* the same hatch is useful for purely-local "I want this input shaped differently" cases. One mechanism, many uses.

**How to apply:** When the design needs an override knob on the cross-language path, propose "custom translation spec on the destination port" rather than inventing per-function annotations, type discriminator metadata, or producer-side conversion hints (all three were rejected — see feedback_cross_language_pitfalls). The port is the unit of override; the spec is user code; the rest stays default.

```

### project_editor_visual_language.md

```markdown
---
name: Editor visual language for wires
description: Wire color in the canvas editor encodes language pairing across the edge, not just routing kind — a UI invariant future work should respect (issue 245)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**Wires are colored by language pairing across the edge**, with a separate color for wires whose destination port carries a user-written custom translation (issue 246). Pre-245 wires were colored purely by routing kind (default slate-blue, comparator branches orange/blue/green).

**The pairing-based palette:**
- **Same-language hop** — the wire carries native bytes; default neutral color.
- **Cross-language hop (forest green, ~`#228b22`)** — different producer/consumer languages; runtime translates via JSON at the wire. The color is a standing reminder that encode + decode is happening on that hop.
- **Custom-translation hop** — a third distinct color signaling the destination port has a user-written translation spec overriding the default path.
- Branch-routing colors (orange/blue/green from comparator boxes) compose on top — routing kind and language pairing are orthogonal axes the editor must show simultaneously.

**Why:** The runtime treats same-lang and cross-lang hops very differently (dual-ring slot design, issue 312), but pre-245 the editor gave the box author no visual signal that the JSON translation step existed. It was invisible until someone read the dispatch code. Translation cost should be legible from the canvas.

**How to apply:** Any future editor work that touches wire rendering must preserve "color encodes language pairing." Don't propose recoloring schemes that overload the cross-language signal onto another concept. New routing concepts get new axes (line style, glyphs, animation) rather than stealing color. When discussing wire visuals, name both axes — routing kind AND language pairing — even if only one is changing.

```

### project_encapsulated_map.md

```markdown
---
name: Encapsulated map as box
description: A sub-map opens as a single box on a parent canvas. Data boxes marked externally-supplied become input ports; write boxes marked externally-consumed become output ports. The documented exception to single-output-per-box (issue 248, amended 2026-05-23)
type: project
originSessionId: 1228a221-1c09-4c26-94f3-172d7777b2b9
---
**A map directory has two ways to be opened:** as the top-level graph (existing map-select UI), or as an **encapsulated box** on the currently-edited parent map (issue 248). Opening through the file browser while a parent map is open instantiates the sub-map as a single box on the parent's canvas.

**The encapsulation contract — symmetric input and output toggles:**
- **Inputs:** any `data` box inside the sub-map can be toggled "externally-supplied" in its inspector. Each such box becomes a typed input port on the encapsulated box.
- **Outputs:** any `write` box inside the sub-map can be toggled "externally-consumed" in its inspector. Each such box surfaces as a **distinct output port** on the encapsulated box. A write box with the toggle on can still write to its `path` if one is set — the file destination and the parent-wire destination are independent.

**Encapsulated maps are the documented exception to issue 218's "single output per box" rule.** They have *N* output ports — one per externally-consumed write box, where *N* may be zero (pure side-effect map), one, or many. Every other box kind still has exactly one output.

**Rejected earlier design (2026-05-21):** packing all write-box outputs into a single byte-blob with a leading null-terminated size index, single wire out. Rejected 2026-05-23 because it would have repurposed file-writing machinery to emit strings into wires — substituting one mechanism for another. The symmetric toggle design preserves the `write` box's "terminate a value" semantics and treats the destination kind as a mode toggle.

**Why:** Encapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph. The parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals — it sees declared input ports, declared output ports, and known semantics. Sub-maps can be edited independently, reused across parents, and packaged once for distribution. This is the closest SoraMech gets to "user-defined functions" while staying graph-native.

**How to apply:** When discussing map composition, reuse, or "how do users build libraries of behavior" — encapsulation is the answer. Don't propose alternative function-abstraction mechanisms (named subgraphs as text references, macro-style inlining, blob-packed outputs) without explicitly weighing them against the symmetric-toggle shape. Both toggles (`externally-supplied` on data boxes, `externally-consumed` on write boxes) are the user-facing port-declaration mechanism — don't invent a separate "ports manifest" file.

```

### project_soramech.md

```markdown
---
name: SoraMech project context
description: Core architecture decisions, file layout, and execution model for SoraMech, across phase 2 (current) and phase 3 (designed)
type: project
originSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a
---
SoraMech is a visual FSM/dataflow editor and execution engine at /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/.

**Why:** Primary use case is LLM orchestration on the SoraMind Alpine cluster. Strings flow between boxes like variables. History is explicit, loaded from disk only when a box needs it.

**Three independent programs sharing a map directory:**
- `src/006-server-main.lua` — thin HTTP file CRUD proxy. No runner management.
- Runner — phase 2: `src/007-runner-main.lua` (synchronous Lua). Phase 3: `soramech-pool` (C binary, designed in issues 301–311, not yet built).
- `assets/index.html` — vanilla JS canvas editor. Editor only — no run button. Compile button (issue 222) is a phase 2 placeholder; it triggers the phase 3 build pipeline (issue 219).

**Key architecture decisions (current truth):**
- Each box is its own JSON file in `boxes/<id>.json`. Connections written to BOTH endpoint files; loader validates both ends agree — hard error if not.
- **Single output wire per box** (issue 218 complete). No `outputs` array. The function returns one value; routing is by `from_branch` on the connection.
- **Comparator-based branching** (issue 210) — replaces the earlier `branch` box kind with named ports. A box may carry a `comparand`; the dispatch layer fires `lt`/`eq`/`gt` connections. No spec is invoked for comparators.
- **Iterator boxes** (issue 221) — pure routing primitives, no `ref`/`fn`. Dispatch layer cycles through `iterator_outputs` based on a per-task counter.
- **Phase 2 drivers** are shell scripts under `drivers/` (one process per call, stdout as channel). **Phase 3 language specs** are `.so` libraries under `langs/<name>/spec.so` loaded via `dlopen` (issue 303). Lua and C are in-process; Bash is out-of-process via Unix domain socket.
- Data files: per-map JSON in `data/`. Section-level `constant` flag. Accessed via `libs/soramech-data.lua`.
- State/ephemeral: `tmp/` is a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Phase 2 writes `last-run.json` (single doc). Phase 3 writes `last-run.jsonl` (JSON Lines, issue 311) — decoupled from the editor, consumed by LLMs / CLI viewers / test harness.
- **Phase 3 runtime model**: C pool runner owns a 3d-rts task pool; per-task slots in process heap (issue 302) with refcounting and a separate large-value heap; dispatch layer (304) is the worker action; graph loader is C (305), no embedded Lua at the runner level. Phase 2's synchronous executor retires when phase 3 lands.

**How to apply:** When working on any component, respect the three-way separation. Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server. Map directory format is the only shared contract. The phase 2 driver model and the phase 3 spec model coexist conceptually (phase 2 is current, phase 3 is fully designed) but the runtime mechanism differs entirely; box JSON and the editor are unchanged across the cutover.

```

### project_threading.md

```markdown
---
name: threading_model
description: SoraMech's threading model — phase 2 synchronous, phase 3 SoraMech-owned C thread pool with per-port slots and language specs
type: project
originSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a
---
**Phase 2 (current)**: synchronous executor in `src/004-executor.lua`. Single-threaded, sequential box execution. One driver shell-out per box call. The phase 2 path goes away when phase 3 lands — no fallback, no coroutine intermediate.

**Phase 3 (designed, not yet built)**: C pool runner with a SoraMech-owned thread pool. The 3d-rts pool at `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` is the **design reference**, not vendored — SoraMech owns its pool implementation so the spawn primitive, worker context, init barrier, and iterator-pinning extensions are all under our control. The architecture is fully specified across issues 301–313.

Key phase 3 concepts:
- **Per-input-port slots** (not per-task), allocated at graph load and durable for the run. Each slot is a ring buffer (`n_cells` cells of `cell_capacity` bytes). 1-cell slots use peek-not-drain (literals, single-push wires); N-cell slots use pop-and-drain (queued / multi-push wires). No per-slot refcounting — slot lifetime is the whole run.
- **Tasks are ephemeral**: spawned dynamically by the dispatch layer when a box's input set is ready. Tasks carry just `box_id` and a counter snapshot. Box state (counter, input slots, language handle) is durable.
- **Language specs** under `langs/<name>/spec.so`, loaded via `dlopen` at startup. Uniform `lang_spec_t`. No language is privileged.
- **Same-language fast path** (issue 312): wire format defaults to JSON, but two adjacent same-language boxes use the language's native serialization (Lua `lua_dump`, C struct memcpy). Compile-time wire classification picks the path.
- **In-process specs** (Lua, C) via `lua_pcall` / `dlsym`. **Out-of-process specs** (Bash) via Unix domain sockets to a persistent per-worker subprocess.
- **Dispatch layer** (304) is the worker-side action: pop inputs → branch on box mode → invoke spec → push to downstream input slots → end. No blocking, no wait lists; tasks spawn on input arrival and run to completion.
- **Iterator and comparator routing** in the dispatch layer. Comparator runs the function and routes by output value. Iterator skips the function and routes by per-box counter (atomic spawn-time increment). Iterator tasks parallelize across workers; ordering preserved via per-push counter tags on consumer slots.
- **No-null rule** (issue 230): every input port must be wired, given a literal, or marked optional. Compile fails on missing inputs.
- **Init barrier**: pool startup waits until every worker has run every spec's `init(worker_idx)` before submitting tasks. Avoids tasks landing on uninitialized handles.
- **Hard-crash error policy**: nonzero return from any spec aborts the program.
- **Blocking semantics**: long-running operations tie up a worker. Pool size is the budget. Cooperative split (kickoff + check-done iterator) avoids holding a worker. See `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.

**Effil is explicitly NOT used.** Coroutines are not used. The C pool is the chosen mechanism. 3d-rts is referenced as design inspiration, not vendored.

**How to apply:** When discussing threading, parallelism, or cross-language IPC: phase 2 is synchronous shell-out drivers; phase 3 is the SoraMech-owned C pool runner with `lang_spec_t`, per-port slot stores, and dispatch-layer routing. Never suggest effil. 3d-rts is a reference, not a dependency. Issues 301–313 carry the design.

```

    "content":"hi, can you initialize a project here? The goal is to create a thin web client with an infinite scrolling canvas that the user can make box-diagrams on and connect them. Essentially a finite state machine. This FSM should be loaded from text files that are local on the computer defined in json. Each box should do something - run a function in one of the files in the SRC directory within the directory where we're storing the FSM structural files. It could be a function in a library (only public functions of course) like in C, or it could be a bash script or something. We want to be agnostic to what the user wants to do. We should also be able to create data files that include things like structs and such. For now, let's build for lua only functionality - storing tables in data files with json using dkjson, and doing all of the control flow with lua. The web application should simply be a UI to manipulate the local files, but we might later implement an HTTP server that lets a user control it remotely or something like that - open to discussion. We want simple control flow, with if/then/else, for loops, and anything else that seems reasonable. The user should be able to create multiple of these \"maps\" and they should be callable from one-another (but for now let's just keep them separate) which means they each will need their own output directory. What do you think?"
  },

Main tradeoff: pure-static-file editor (open `index.html` directly, use File System Access API) is simpler but Chromium-only and clunky for shell-script invocation; a tiny lua server is more setup but lets the editor *also* run the FSM and stream output back, which seems closer to what you want.\n\nA few things I'd want pinned down before writing the vision doc:\n\n1. **What does a \"box\" actually contain at rest?** A reference like `{kind=\"lua\", file=\"src/foo.lua\", fn=\"do_thing\"}` plus a typed input/output port list? {

        "type":"text",
        "text":"Good answers — I think we're ~80% of the way to a vision doc. Let me unpack Q2 and react.\n\n**Q2 explained.** Two extremes:\n\n- *Shared context* — one big table `ctx` lives for the whole run. Every box receives `ctx`, mutates fields on it, returns only a transition label like `\"ok\"` or `\"fail\"`. Wiring between boxes is implicit: box B reads whatever box A wrote into `ctx`. Easy to add a new field, painful to see what flows where (it's all invisible in the diagram).\n- *Dataflow / wired ports* — each box declares its input args and its return values as named ports. Wires literally connect output port of A to input port of B. A box can only see what's wired into its inputs. The diagram *is* the data flow — nothing hidden.\n\nYour Q1 + Q3 answers already pick dataflow: structured input args parsed into the UI, tuple returns as multiple output ports, conditionals routing on those values. That's the wired-ports world. **The per-map data files (Q4) then play the role of the \"shared context\" for things that shouldn't be threaded through every wire** — e.g. the running LLM chat history, accumulated tool results, scratch memory. Boxes call `data.get(\"conversation\")` / `data.set(...)` to read/write. Best of both: explicit wires for the values that matter at this step, named data store for state that persists across many steps.\n\n**Q3 — where conditionals live.** Three options, in order of how I'd rank them for your case:\n\n1. **Predicates on wires.** Each output port can have multiple outgoing wires; each wire carries a small structured condition (comparator dropdown: `== > < contains matches is-nil`, plus a literal or another port reference). Runtime walks wires from the port and follows the ones whose predicate is true. UI shows a little tag on the wire (`> 4`). No new box type. Matches your \"if greater than 4, run this box next\" almost literally.\n2. **Branch box (dedicated kind).** A `branch` box takes one input, has N output ports each with a condition slot. Cleaner diagrams when there are many cases (switch-style), but it's a new kind and feels redundant with #1 for the common 2-way case.\n3. **Both.** Wires support simple predicates; branch box exists for big switches. Probably where we end up eventually but I'd start with #1 only and add #2 if it earns its keep.\n\n**Q4 reaction.** Per-map memory + a small `data` API exposed to box functions feels right. We can have two flavors of data file: *constants* (read-only, loaded at start) and *state* (read/write, persisted on shutdown or on explicit `save` from a box). Both are json tables on disk in the map's directory.\n\n**Q5 reaction.** Your tradition fits cleanly: every map has `output/` with a `logs/` subdir that's a symlink into `/tmp/<map>-logs/`, while `output/data/` (or similar) holds the long-term json the user explicitly chose to persist. I'd add a `output/runs/` for last-run snapshot json — useful for debugging without bloating the long-term store.\n\n**One more thing** the LLM-orchestration angle surfaces: a lot of LLM calls are *async / slow*. Two ways to handle:\n- Synchronous for v1 — boxes just block; the engine runs single-threaded and you watch progress in the UI. Simplest. Plays nicely with later swapping in the 3d-rts thread pool when it's ready.\n- Coroutine-based from day one — every box is a coroutine, the runtime can have several \"in flight\" and a node only fires when all its input ports are filled. This is the dataflow-graph way and it's how you'd want it once threading lands. More upfront design.\n\nGiven your \"don't worry about those too much yet\" — I'd start synchronous, but design the box-call boundary so each box is `function(inputs) -> outputs` with no global side effects beyond the `data` API. That makes the later coroutine/thread-pool swap a runtime change, not a rewrite.\n\nSo my proposed direction to lock in before writing `notes/vision`:\n\n- Boxes = structured `{kind, ref, inputs[], outputs[]}` with multi-output for tuples; UI fully parses/edits these\n- Wires = `from_port → to_port`, optional structured predicate on the wire\n- Per-map `data/` = read/write json tables, accessed by boxes via a small `data` API\n- Per-map `output/` with `logs → /tmp/...` symlink, `runs/` for last-run, `data/` for persisted state\n- Engine v1 = synchronous lua; thin localhost lua HTTP server backs the web editor and also runs the FSM\n- LLM orchestration is the north star use case — strings flowing through wires, history in `data/`\n\nTwo final yes/no questions and I'll start scaffolding:\n\n**A.** OK with predicates-on-wires (option #1) for v1, defer branch-box?\n**B.** OK with synchronous engine for v1, coroutine/thread-pool later when 3d-rts's pool is usable?\n\nAnd one I genuinely don't know your answer to:\n\n**C.** For the box \"function reference\" — should a box be allowed to invoke a function from a *library* file (`src/lib/strings.lua` → public function `trim`), a function from a *local* file (`src/my-thing.lua` → `do_thing`), AND a shell command, all from day one? Or start lua-only (both library + local) and add shell later? Shell adds an escaping/IO surface that's worth deferring if you're not sure you need it on day one."

Best of both: explicit wires for the values that matter at this step, named data store for\n  state that persists across many steps.\n\nwe're going to want to make some functions for such a thing, but they will be library functions and so are imported and utilized the same as any other library we're using.\n\n  2. Branch box (dedicated kind). A branch box takes one input, has N output ports each with a condition slot. Cleaner diagrams when there are many cases (switch-style), but it's a new kind and feels redundant with #1 for the common 2-way case.\n\nlet's do a dedicated box for it. Many of the predicate tests we're going to be doing are going to be passed through an LLM - \"is this more rogue or wizard\" would have three outputs, rogue, wizard, or else. \"can this be integrated into our datastructure? [datastructure_context_data_file]\" would have two outputs, yes, no, and any \"else\" outputs would be routed back into the same node to run again, this time with different LLM variables like temperature or creativity or whatever. These values will be pseudo-randomized, to give a different perspective on the same problem.\n\n  Q4 reaction. Per-map memory + a small data API exposed to box functions feels right. We can have two flavors of data file: constants (read-only, loaded at start) and state (read/write, persisted on shutdown or on explicit save from a box). Both are json tables on disk in the map's directory.\n\nstate should be stored in the /tmp/ symlink directory. Anything else should be written to disk. If something is intended to be constant, as in read-only, then it should be defined as such in a language like C or lua or bash - idk, does bash have constant values? Right now we only need to support C and Lua - sometimes, defining datastructures or even just data in general in C is easier than in json. Alternatively, actually this might be better, just have a flag in the json datafile that marks whether it's constant or not. Or rather, if a particular section of the datafile is constant teehee\n\nI'd add a output/runs/ for last-run snapshot json — useful for\n  debugging without bloating the long-term store.\n\nwe can store this with the state mentioned above. in a /tmp/ directory.\n\n  One more thing the LLM-orchestration angle surfaces: a lot of LLM calls are async / slow. Two ways to handle:\n  - Synchronous for v1 — boxes just block; the engine runs single-threaded and you watch progress in the UI. Simplest. Plays nicely with later swapping in the 3d-rts thread pool when it's ready.\n  - Coroutine-based from day one — every box is a coroutine, the runtime can have several \"in flight\" and a node only fires when all its input ports are filled. This is the dataflow-graph way and it's how you'd want it once threading lands. More upfront design.\n\n\nread the thread pool implementation. It's not done yet, and it's had... SEVERAL iterations, so make sure you're on the up-to-date version. Let's start synchronous though since that's still in development, but design it such that each operation is calling a \"task\" or something so that we can easily transition to the threadpool system.\n\n  C. For the box \"function reference\" — should a box be allowed to invoke a function from a library file (src/lib/strings.lua → public function trim), a function from a local file (src/my-thing.lua → do_thing), AND a shell command, all from day one? Or start lua-only (both library +\n  local) and add shell later? Shell adds an escaping/IO surface that's worth deferring if you're not sure you need it on day one.\n\nCalling a function from a library file should be as simple as \"src/strings.lua/trim()\". The shell script is also easy because it'd just be \"src/trim.sh\". We need both. If the user is calling a C program, it'd be \"src/string.c/trim()\" - note how we're not referring to a compiled binary. We could do that, if we referred to it like a shell script, but in the case that we call into the header file / library .c file, we'll need to first check whether or not we have compiled that file since it was last modified. If no, then we compile it at runtime. If yes, then we just treat it like a lua library file.\n\nSo, I see two paths for calling functions. Either we're referring to a binary (or a shell script, something atomic-ish) or we're pointing at an SRC file and asking the map to figure out how to run / call it. Right now, we only need to support C, bash, and lua, but we should have a system so that a user can define custom methods for these things. Like, \"if you want to use rust or go or haskell or something, run this shell script\" and the user would have to write it themselves to define how the compilation / interpretation process works. This should be a first-class scenario, as in, soemthing we expect the user to use for their language of choice. We should try and be agnostic."
  },

        "content":"1\t# 123 — Task pool: library-managed periodics (frame-based)\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\t\n5\t**Superseded by issue 127.** Captured during the iter4 design\n6\tconversation (2026-04-28). After 107's snap problem surfaced\n7\t(2026-04-29), the design pivoted from a dedicated \"periodics\"\n8\tabstraction to a more general **frame-ring scheduling** model\n9\t(issue 127). Periodics fall out for free under that design as a\n10\tone-line idiom: a self-rescheduling task calls\n11\t`pool_spawn_in(N, ...)` in its reschedule action to run every N\n12\tframes.\n13\t\n14\tThe remainder of this file is preserved as design history.\n15\t\n16\t## Why frames, not microseconds\n17\t\n18\tEarlier conversation suggested microseconds. On reflection, frames\n19\tare the right unit:\n20\t\n21\t- Game cadence is frame-bound, not wall-time-bound. A task that\n22\t  needs to \"run roughly every render tick\" is naturally expressed\n23\t  in frames.\n24\t- Frame counters are monotonic, cheap to read, and don't require\n25\t  `clock_gettime` syscalls.\n26\t- The cycler's natural rhythm is already discrete; frames map onto\n27\t  it cleanly.\n28\t\n29\t## Current behavior\n30\t\n31\tThere is no library notion of periodicity. A task that wants to\n32\tre-run periodically does so manually: at the end of its action\n33\tchain, it calls `pool_spawn` to create the next iteration.\n34\t\n35\tSelf-rescheduling tasks must:\n36\t1. Decide their own next-iteration priority.\n37\t2. Track their own arrival timestamps if they care about latency.\n38\t3. Re-spawn with all the same actions and args each time.\n39\t\n40\tThis works but is repetitive boilerplate at every periodic site.\n41\t\n42\t## Intended behavior\n43\t\n44\tThe library accepts a per-task periodicity spec at spawn time:\n45\t\n46\t```c\n47\ttypedef struct {\n48\t    int every_n_frames;     // target cadence: re-run every N frames.\n49\t    int max_slack_frames;   // if a run is more than this many frames late,\n50\t                            //   library promotes priority by one for the\n51\t                            //   next iteration (sticky until a run lands\n52\t                            //   on time again).\n53\t    int floor_priority;     // never auto-promote past this.\n54\t} task_periodic_spec_t;\n55\t\n56\ttask_id_t pool_spawn_periodic(task_pool_t *pool,\n57\t                               const action_fn_t *actions,\n58\t                               void *const      *action_args,\n59\t                               int               n_actions,\n60\t                               int               initial_priority,\n61\t                               task_periodic_spec_t  spec);\n62\t```\n63\t\n64\tThe library:\n65\t\n66\t1. Increments a frame counter on each frame boundary (driven by the\n67\t   game loop calling `pool_advance_frame(pool)`).\n68\t2. Tracks the last-completion frame number for each periodic task.\n69\t3. When a periodic task completes, schedules a re-spawn at frame\n70\t   `last_completion + every_n_frames`. The re-spawn happens by\n71\t   inserting a marker into a per-frame \"due\" list.\n72\t4. If the actual completion frame exceeds the target by more than\n73\t   `max_slack_frames`, bumps `initial_priority` by one for the\n74\t   next spawn (sticky promotion until the task starts landing on\n75\t   time again).\n76\t5. Auto-demote-on-block (already in iter4) still applies.\n77\t\n78\t## Suggested implementation steps\n79\t\n80\t1. Add `int frame` field to `task_pool_t`. Add\n81\t   `void pool_advance_frame(task_pool_t *pool)` — called by the\n82\t   game loop once per render tick.\n83\t2. Add `task_periodic_spec_t` typedef and `pool_spawn_periodic`\n84\t   public API.\n85\t3. Internally, periodic tasks have an extra \"rescheduler\" action\n86\t   appended to their actions array (similar in spirit to the\n87\t   iter3-era synthetic dep-check, but for re-spawning rather than\n88\t   waiting). The rescheduler computes the next spawn frame and\n89\t   priority based on this iteration's actual completion frame\n90\t   versus target.\n91\t4. The pool maintains a small \"frame-ordered due list\" — tasks\n92\t   waiting for their target frame to arrive. Each call to\n93\t   `pool_advance_frame` walks tasks whose target frame ≤ current,\n94\t   pushes them onto the ready queue at their current priority.\n95\t5. Update `tests/000-index.md` blind-spot list to remove\n96\t   \"periodics\" once tests cover this.\n97\t\n98\t## Tests\n99\t\n100\t- `tests/NN-task-pool-periodic-cadence.c` — periodic at cadence\n101\t  N; assert it runs ~`total_frames / N` times across a fixed\n102\t  number of frame advances.\n103\t- `tests/NN-task-pool-periodic-slack-promote.c` — periodic with\n104\t  small `max_slack_frames` under artificial load; assert priority\n105\t  rises after slack is exceeded.\n106\t\n107\t## Related\n108\t\n109\t- `114-coroutine-pool-library.md` — the deferred `promote_if_late`\n110\t  flag idea originated there. This issue subsumes it.\n111\t- `107-unit-movement-on-terrain.md` — likely the first periodic\n112\t  consumer (per-tick movement update). When 107 transitions onto\n113\t  the pool, its requirements will pin down details here.\n114\t\n115\t## Out of scope\n116\t\n117\t- Wall-time-based periodicity. If real-time deadlines matter\n118\t  (e.g., audio), a separate mechanism applies; this one is for\n119\t  game-tick cadence.\n120\t- Adaptive cadence (e.g., \"run more often when there's load to\n121\t  spare\"). Initial design is fixed-N; adaptive can come later.\n122\t",

      "content":"# 123 — Task pool: library-managed periodics (frame-based)\n\n## Status\n\n**Superseded by issue 127.** Captured during the iter4 design\nconversation (2026-04-28). After 107's snap problem surfaced\n(2026-04-29), the design pivoted from a dedicated \"periodics\"\nabstraction to a more general **frame-ring scheduling** model\n(issue 127). Periodics fall out for free under that design as a\none-line idiom: a self-rescheduling task calls\n`pool_spawn_in(N, ...)` in its reschedule action to run every N\nframes.\n\nThe remainder of this file is preserved as design history.\n\n## Why frames, not microseconds\n\nEarlier conversation suggested microseconds. On reflection, frames\nare the right unit:\n\n- Game cadence is frame-bound, not wall-time-bound. A task that\n  needs to \"run roughly every render tick\" is naturally expressed\n  in frames.\n- Frame counters are monotonic, cheap to read, and don't require\n  `clock_gettime` syscalls.\n- The cycler's natural rhythm is already discrete; frames map onto\n  it cleanly.\n\n## Current behavior\n\nThere is no library notion of periodicity. A task that wants to\nre-run periodically does so manually: at the end of its action\nchain, it calls `pool_spawn` to create the next iteration.\n\nSelf-rescheduling tasks must:\n1. Decide their own next-iteration priority.\n2. Track their own arrival timestamps if they care about latency.\n3. Re-spawn with all the same actions and args each time.\n\nThis works but is repetitive boilerplate at every periodic site.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nThe library accepts a per-task periodicity spec at spawn time:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    int every_n_frames;     // target cadence: re-run every N frames.\n    int max_slack_frames;   // if a run is more than this many frames late,\n                            //   library promotes priority by one for the\n                            //   next iteration (sticky until a run lands\n                            //   on time again).\n    int floor_priority;     // never auto-promote past this.\n} task_periodic_spec_t;\n\ntask_id_t pool_spawn_periodic(task_pool_t *pool,\n                               const action_fn_t *actions,\n                               void *const      *action_args,\n                               int               n_actions,\n                               int               initial_priority,\n                               task_periodic_spec_t  spec);\n```\n\nThe library:\n\n1. Increments a frame counter on each frame boundary (driven by the\n   game loop calling `pool_advance_frame(pool)`).\n2. Tracks the last-completion frame number for each periodic task.\n3. When a periodic task completes, schedules a re-spawn at frame\n   `last_completion + every_n_frames`. The re-spawn happens by\n   inserting a marker into a per-frame \"due\" list.\n4. If the actual completion frame exceeds the target by more than\n   `max_slack_frames`, bumps `initial_priority` by one for the\n   next spawn (sticky promotion until the task starts landing on\n   time again).\n5. Auto-demote-on-block (already in iter4) still applies.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. Add `int frame` field to `task_pool_t`. Add\n   `void pool_advance_frame(task_pool_t *pool)` — called by the\n   game loop once per render tick.\n2. Add `task_periodic_spec_t` typedef and `pool_spawn_periodic`\n   public API.\n3. Internally, periodic tasks have an extra \"rescheduler\" action\n   appended to their actions array (similar in spirit to the\n   iter3-era synthetic dep-check, but for re-spawning rather than\n   waiting). The rescheduler computes the next spawn frame and\n   priority based on this iteration's actual completion frame\n   versus target.\n4. The pool maintains a small \"frame-ordered due list\" — tasks\n   waiting for their target frame to arrive. Each call to\n   `pool_advance_frame` walks tasks whose target frame ≤ current,\n   pushes them onto the ready queue at their current priority.\n5. Update `tests/000-index.md` blind-spot list to remove\n   \"periodics\" once tests cover this.\n\n## Tests\n\n- `tests/NN-task-pool-periodic-cadence.c` — periodic at cadence\n  N; assert it runs ~`total_frames / N` times across a fixed\n  number of frame advances.\n- `tests/NN-task-pool-periodic-slack-promote.c` — periodic with\n  small `max_slack_frames` under artificial load; assert priority\n  rises after slack is exceeded.\n\n## Related\n\n- `114-coroutine-pool-library.md` — the deferred `promote_if_late`\n  flag idea originated there. This issue subsumes it.\n- `107-unit-movement-on-terrain.md` — likely the first periodic\n  consumer (per-tick movement update). When 107 transitions onto\n  the pool, its requirements will pin down details here.\n\n## Out of scope\n\n- Wall-time-based periodicity. If real-time deadlines matter\n  (e.g., audio), a separate mechanism applies; this one is for\n  game-tick cadence.\n- Adaptive cadence (e.g., \"run more often when there's load to\n  spare\"). Initial design is fixed-N; adaptive can come later.\n",
      "startLine":1,
      "totalLines":122,
      "filePath":"/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/issues/123-task-pool-periodics.md",
      "numLines":122
    }

}

Direct successor\n6\tto issue 123 (which is now superseded — periodics are subsumed by\n7\tthis design as \"schedule into frame N+k\").\n8\t\n9\t## Why this exists\n10\t\n11\tIssue 107's Shape B movement (per-unit self-rescheduling tasks at\n12\tpriority 2) exposed a fundamental architectural problem with\n13\tself-rescheduling-at-max-rate: **timestamp-based motion is\n14\tmathematically correct under variable cadence, but cadence\n15\tvariability is unbounded.** A worker thread can be off-CPU for\n16\t1-3 seconds when the system is contended; when it resumes, the\n17\tunit's next step has to cover that real-time delta in one frame.\n18\tThe result is a visual snap from old position to new position,\n19\twith no smooth interpolation.\n20\t\n21\tThis is not a small bug. It's the architecture announcing that\n22\t\"poll as fast as possible, math will fix it\" doesn't work when\n23\tthe underlying scheduling is non-uniform. The fix is to bound\n24\tcadence variability — make `dt` approximately constant by\n25\tlocking task execution to frame boundaries.\n26\t\n27\t## Snap reproduction (motivating example, captured 2026-04-29)\n28\t\n29\t- 6 units, press T, all get random targets via\n30\t  `units_set_target` → `pool_spawn` per unit.\n31\t- 5 units move smoothly toward their new targets.\n32\t- 1 unit stays visually stationary for 1-3 seconds, then snaps\n33\t  (instantly translates and rotates) to a new position.\n34\t- Fans run at full speed while units are moving.\n35\t\n36\tRoot cause: in `move_advance`, `now = GetTime()` is captured at\n37\tthe start of the action; the action does its arithmetic; at the\n38\tend, `u->last_update_t = now` writes that *start-of-action* `now`\n39\tvalue. If the OS preempts the worker between the capture and the\n40\twrite (as happens occasionally on a contended system), real-time\n41\tadvances during the preemption but the captured `now` does not.\n42\tThe next iteration sees `dt = GetTime() - last_update_t` of 1-3\n43\tseconds, computes a correct-but-large step, and the unit teleports.\n44\t\n45\tNo band-aid in this layer fixes the issue without losing physical\n46\tcorrectness:\n47\t- \"Read GetTime() at end of action\" → drops the preempted time;\n48\t  unit covers less total distance.\n49\t- \"Cap dt at 100ms\" → same thing, more aggressively.\n50\t\n51\tThe only correct fix: bound how often the action runs. If\n52\tmovement runs exactly once per frame and frame rate is bounded\n53\t(`SetTargetFPS(60)`), `dt ≈ 16.67ms ± small jitter`. No\n54\taccumulation, no snap, no lost distance.\n55\t\n56\t## Intended design\n57\t\n58\tA **ring of frame slots**, each slot itself containing the same\n59\tten priority queues we have today. Concretely on `task_pool_t`:\n60\t\n61\t```c\n62\t#define FRAME_RING_SIZE 8        // tunable — how many frames of lookahead\n63\tstruct task_pool {\n64\t    // ... existing fields except the queue arrays ...\n65\t    struct {\n66\t        struct task **queues[N_PRIORITIES + 1];\n67\t        int queue_lens[N_PRIORITIES + 1];\n68\t        int queue_caps[N_PRIORITIES + 1];\n69\t        int n_ready_total;\n70\t    } frames[FRAME_RING_SIZE];\n71\t    int current_frame;             // index into frames[]; the slot workers drain.\n72\t    int next_frame_offset;         // == 1 typically — \"next frame\" is current+1 mod size.\n73\t};\n74\t```\n75\t\n76\tWorkers only pop from `frames[current_frame]`. New spawns always\n77\tland in `frames[(current_frame + offset) % FRAME_RING_SIZE]`,\n78\twhere `offset >= 1` (the rule below).\n79\t\n80\t### Spawning rules\n81\t\n82\t- **`pool_spawn(...)`** — implicit \"schedule for next frame.\"\n83\t  Lands in `frames[(current_frame + 1) % SIZE]`. Cannot land in\n84\t  the current frame; mid-frame work is what *this* frame's tasks\n85\t  scheduled *previously*, not what just-spawned tasks request.\n86\t- **`pool_spawn_in(N, ...)`** — schedule N frames from now. N=1\n87\t  is the default. N=0 is rejected (or interpreted as N=1; TBD).\n88\t  N=2 is \"two frames out.\" N is *relative*, never an absolute\n89\t  frame counter — relative makes sense regardless of how many\n90\t  frames have run, doesn't require user to track a global counter.\n91\t- **`pool_spawn_in_current(...)`** — escape hatch for code that\n92\t  legitimately wants to land in the current frame (e.g., a task\n93\t  that needs to react to user input *this* frame, like a click\n94\t  handler). Used sparingly. Could be omitted entirely from the\n95\t  initial implementation if we don't need it.\n96\t\n97\t### Frame advance\n98\t\n99\tMain thread calls `pool_advance_frame(pool)` after the render\n100\tloop's `EndDrawing()` to mark \"this frame is done; please move on.\"\n101\t\n102\tTwo possible behaviors when the current slot still has unfinished\n103\twork:\n104\t\n105\t1. **Stall (recommended).** `pool_advance_frame` blocks until the\n106\t   current slot is fully drained (n_ready_total == 0 across all\n107\t   priorities AND no parked tasks waiting on tasks in this slot).\n108\t   Main thread keeps rendering — animations, particles, camera\n109\t   pan — but game-logic frame doesn't advance until this frame's\n110\t   logic is done. This is the model that makes lockstep multiplayer\n111\t   determinism possible: all clients agree on logic-frame N's\n112\t   complete state before advancing to N+1.\n113\t\n114\t2. Auto-promote leftover tasks to next frame. Simpler, but mixes\n115\t   frame budgets and breaks determinism. Rejected.\n116\t\n117\tStall behavior is preferred. If the game routinely overflows its\n118\tframe budget, that's a profiling problem, not a scheduling one —\n119\tfix it by speeding up the offending tasks.\n120\t\n121\t### Multiplayer determinism (motivating future use case)\n122\t\n123\tFrame-locked task execution means: given the same input at the\n124\tstart of frame N, all clients produce the same end-of-frame N\n125\tstate. Clients can't have one client's logic \"race ahead\" because\n126\tits CPU is faster — every client waits for its own frame N tasks\n127\tto drain before advancing. Then they exchange inputs for frame\n128\tN+1. Standard lockstep model. The frame-ring design is the natural\n129\tfit; a polling pool would have to be retrofitted.\n130\t\n131\t## What stays the same\n132\t\n133\t- Public API for action contracts (`task_ctx_t`, `action_fn_t`,\n134\t  `ACT_*` enum values, `slot_status_t`).\n135\t- Parking on blocked-target (iter4.5 semantics). Parked tasks are\n136\t  not in any frame slot; they're attached to their blocker's\n137\t  waiters list. When woken, they get pushed to a frame's queue\n138\t  (current frame? next frame? — design decision pending).\n139\t- Result-slot semantics, refcounting, registry.\n140\t\n141\t## What changes\n142\t\n143\t- `pool_spawn` signature gains a \"frame offset\" or grows\n144\t  `pool_spawn_in(offset, ...)` as a sibling. Default is `+1`.\n145\t- `pool_advance_frame` is new public API.\n146\t- The \"queue\" inside `task_pool_t` becomes per-frame. Internal\n147\t  representation grows; public API barely changes.\n148\t- Self-rescheduling tasks (movement) call `pool_spawn_in(1, ...)`\n149\t  in their reschedule action. Each iteration runs once per frame.\n150\t- The cycler runs *within* a single frame's queues, not across\n151\t  frames. Same logic, just per-slot.\n152\t\n153\t## Suggested implementation steps\n154\t\n155\t1. Add `frames[FRAME_RING_SIZE]` to `task_pool_t`. Move the\n156\t   existing per-priority queue fields into the struct.\n157\t2. Add `current_frame` and the offset / advance functions.\n158\t3. Rewrite `queue_push` to accept a target frame (defaults to\n159\t   `current+1`). Workers' `ready_pop_locked` reads from\n160\t   `frames[current_frame]` only.\n161\t4. Add `pool_advance_frame(pool)` that stalls until current\n162\t   slot drains, then bumps `current_frame`.\n163\t5. Update `pool_spawn` signature (and / or add `pool_spawn_in`).\n164\t6. Update `040-game-pool` wrapper to expose the new API.\n165\t7. Update `001-main.c` to call `pool_advance_frame` in the\n166\t   per-frame loop.\n167\t8. Update `050-units.c` so movement reschedule uses\n168\t   `pool_spawn_in(1, ...)`.\n169\t9. Verify: snap is gone. Fans no longer run at full speed during\n170\t   movement (CPU drops to \"6 tasks × 60Hz = 360 iterations/s\"\n171\t   instead of \"hundreds of thousands per second\").\n172\t10. Update tests: rewrite test 005 (priority cycler) to advance\n173\t    frames; add a frame-ring-specific test\n174\t    (`tests/NN-task-pool-frame-bucket.c`).\n175\t\n176\t## Open design questions for implementation time\n177\t\n178\t- **Where do woken parked tasks land?** Current frame (run this\n179\t  frame) or next frame (deferred)? Probably next frame for\n180\t  consistency.\n181\t- **What's the right `FRAME_RING_SIZE`?** 8 is a guess. A periodic\n182\t  scheduling 5 frames out needs SIZE >= 5. Larger sizes cost\n183\t  memory (one set of queue arrays per slot). 16 might be safer\n184\t  default.\n185\t- **`pool_advance_frame` stall semantics under shutdown.** If\n186\t  the pool is shutting down with pending frame work, do we drain\n187\t  or leak? Per `pool_destroy`'s existing contract, leak.\n188\t- **Interaction with promote-on-blocked-target (iter4.5).**\n189\t  Promoting a task from priority 7 to 6 within the same frame\n190\t  works the same. Promotion *across* frames doesn't make sense\n191\t  — a task in next-frame's slot can't be promoted into this\n192\t  frame's queue (we'd race against the drain). Document.\n193\t\n194\t## Related\n195\t\n196\t- `123-task-pool-periodics.md` — superseded by this issue.\n197\t  Periodics (\"run every N frames\") become a one-line idiom under\n198\t  this design: a self-rescheduling task uses `pool_spawn_in(N,\n199\t  ...)` in its reschedule action.\n200\t- `124-task-pool-stable-indices.md` — independent, exploratory.\n201\t  May or may not be wanted; not blocked by this issue.\n202\t- `completed/107-unit-movement-on-terrain.md` — movement is the\n203\t  first real caller; the snap captured here is the motivating\n204\t  problem.\n205\t- `completed/114-coroutine-pool-library.md` — the iter4.5 task\n206\t  pool design that this issue extends.\n207\t\n208\t## Out of scope\n209\t\n210\t- Run-task-end-to-end (no inter-action re-push). If\nmovement runs exactly once per frame and frame rate is bounded\n(`SetTargetFPS(60)`), `dt ≈ 16.67ms ± small jitter`. No\naccumulation, no snap, no lost distance.\n\n## Intended design\n\nA **ring of frame slots**, each slot itself containing the same\nten priority queues we have today.         "content":"1\tSoraMind — Vision\n2\t=================\n3\t\n4\tA camping cluster. Three small Alpine machines at .11, .12, and .13, wired\n5\ttogether on the same gigabit LAN, far from the internet, asked to do\n6\tsomething neat. They do not have to be fast. They have to be alive. The\n7\tpoint of this project is not to ship a product. The point is to design a\n8\tsystem, carefully and deliberately, that runs an LLM-flavored creature on\n9\tthree pooled brains, and to enjoy the process of figuring out exactly how\n10\tevery piece fits.\n11\t\n12\tSoraMind is the mind. It is the inference engine and the research track\n13\tthat explores how a mind of this shape could be built differently. The\n14\tthings the mind ends up powering — a persistent D&D world, an ambient\n15\tnotepad, anything else — live in their own projects that consume SoraMind\n16\tas a substrate. The first such consumer is `narrative-engine`, in a\n17\tsibling directory.\n18\t\n19\tWhy these three boxes?\n20\t----------------------\n21\t\n22\tBecause they are portable, sip power, and make a fine companion in places\n23\twithout coverage. The home desktop, the GPU box, the cloud — those have\n24\ttheir own roles, and Claude and Claude Code remain the tool of choice for\n25\thigh-power focused work at home. The minis exist for a different\n26\trelationship with computation: ambient, meditative, willing to take an\n27\thour to think about whether the bard would lie to the captain of the\n28\tguard. They are good at being slow about things that benefit from being\n29\tslow.\n30\t\n31\tThe deeper goal\n32\t---------------\n33\t\n34\tThis is a software-design project, not a product project. The plan is to\n35\tbuild the inference engine from first principles, in C and LuaJIT,\n36\tdesigned for symmetric three-way distribution from the very first line.\n37\tNo power-of-two constraints inherited from upstream. No layers of someone\n38\telse's design we need to untangle and patch. Every design decision is one\n39\twe made, with a comment explaining why, in a place where future-us can\n40\tfind it.",

Three small Alpine machines at .11, .12, and .13, wired\ntogether on the same gigabit LAN, far from the internet, asked to do\nsomething neat. They do not have to be fast. They have to be alive. The\npoint of this project is not to ship a product. The point is to design a\nsystem, carefully and deliberately, that runs an LLM-flavored creature on\nthree pooled brains, and to enjoy the process of figuring out exactly how\nevery piece fits.\n\nSoraMind is the mind. It is the inference engine and the research track\nthat explores how a mind of this shape could be built differently. The\nthings the mind ends up powering — a persistent D&D world, an ambient\nnotepad, anything else — live in their own projects that consume SoraMind\nas a substrate. The first such consumer is `narrative-engine`, in a\nsibling directory.\n\nWhy these three boxes?\n----------------------\n\nBecause they are portable, sip power, and make a fine companion in places\nwithout coverage. ## [82]

```json
{
  "isSidechain":false,
  "timestamp":"2026-05-07T22:08:40.018Z",
  "gitBranch":"HEAD",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "sessionId":"2029ad16-5678-4b15-931f-3f52d826597a",
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Good. Now I have the full context. Let me consolidate what's locked in before writing the vision:\n\n**Design locked in:**\n\n- **Box** = `{kind, ref, fn, inputs[], outputs[]}`. Two caller kinds: (a) **binary caller** — shell script or binary, run it, get stdout back as outputs; (b) **source caller** — `src/foo.lua/fn`, `src/foo.c/fn` — dispatched through a **language driver**. Built-in drivers: lua/luajit (interpret), bash (run), C (compile on modified, cache binary). User-defined: a shell script the user writes that takes `(file, fn, args...)` and returns results.\n- **Branch box** = dedicated node kind. N named output ports + always an \"else\" port. Routing is string or numeric comparison against output value. \"else\" re-wires to upstream — the retry/randomize logic lives in whatever box feeds the branch, not in the branch box itself.\n- **State**: dataflow wired ports. Per-map json with `constant: true/false` sections. Per-map `tmp/ → /tmp/<map>/` symlink for state + run snapshots. Persistent user data in `output/data/`. Data file access is a lua library (like any other lib), not a built-in API.\n- **v1 sync**: every box call wraps in `task_fn(inputs) -> outputs` — same signature as the pool's action chain — so threading integration is a runtime swap, not a rewrite. effil-jit is available when we're ready.\n- **Libraries at hand**: `dkjson.lua`, `luasocket` (for the HTTP server), `effil-jit` (later). Vanilla JS canvas for the web UI.\n- **North star**: orchestrating SoraMind inference calls on the Alpine cluster — strings as atomic values, text passed between boxes, history in `/tmp/` and explicitly pulled in only when a box needs it.\n\nTwo quick things before I start scaffolding:\n\n**D.** Map file layout — single directory per map with separate files (`nodes.json`, `edges.json`, `data.json`, `drivers.json`) or one big `map.json`? I'd lean toward the split — easier to diff and grep, and each file has a clear single responsibility.\n\n**E.** The web UI canvas — should it load directly as a static `index.html` (File System Access API for reading/writing map files), or does the lua HTTP server always sit between the browser and disk? For local use the server approach is simpler (no browser API quirks, the server can also *run* the FSM and stream output), but it's a daemon you have to start. Fine either way — just confirming that's the direction.\n\nIf both are yes, I'll scaffold right now."
      }],

{
  "isSidechain":false,
  "timestamp":"2026-05-07T22:21:50.522Z",

  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"The difference is **who owns the runner process**.\n\nIn **option 1**, the server forks and execs the runner as its child process. The OS gives you a pipe to its stdout for free. The server knows the PID, can kill it, can wait for it to finish, and gets notified when it exits. Standard parent-child relationship.\n\nIn **option 3**, the runner is launched independently — not a child of the server. It could be started by the user from the terminal, a cron job, another process, anything. The server has no handle on it. The only shared channel is something both parties agree to watch: a file in `/tmp/`, a named pipe (FIFO), or a unix socket. Server polls or `inotify`s the file to know when new output arrives.\n\n**Option 3 is useful when** you want the runner to outlive the server, survive a server restart, or be triggered by something other than the UI. It's also the pattern if the runner is a long-lived daemon rather than a one-shot process.\n\n**For us, since output just goes to files anyway**, the distinction mostly collapses. Option 1 is cleaner for v1: server spawns runner as a child, knows when it's done or crashed, can report that status back to the UI (\"run finished\" / \"run failed with exit code 1\"). The runner writes its outputs to `output/data/` and its logs to `tmp/`. The server doesn't need to proxy anything — it just tracks process state.\n\nOption 3 becomes relevant later if you want to run a map headlessly from a cronjob and still have the UI reflect its status. We can add that without changing the runner — just add a lock file or status json the runner writes to that the server can read on demand.\n\nReady to scaffold?"
      }],

```json
{
  "isSidechain":false,
  "timestamp":"2026-05-07T22:24:46.975Z",
  "gitBranch":"HEAD",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "sessionId":"2029ad16-5678-4b15-931f-3f52d826597a",
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "name":"Write",
        "id":"toolu_01RyqgTNUNfGF2F8LrXBGmfP",
        "type":"tool_use",
        "caller":{
          "type":"direct"
        },
        "input":{
          "content":"SoraMech — Vision\n=================\n\nA visual editor and execution engine for finite state machines built from\ncomposable boxes. Each box is a function call. Boxes are wired together by\nexplicit data connections. The result is a program you can see, edit in a\nbrowser, and run from a terminal — without writing a line of control flow.\n\nThe primary use case is LLM orchestration: wiring inference calls on the\nSoraMind Alpine cluster into coherent multi-step reasoning pipelines.\nStrings are first-class values. Text flows between boxes like water.\nHistory is explicit — loaded from disk only when a box needs it.\n\nWhy this shape?\n---------------\n\nMost orchestration tools hide the wiring. You write code that calls other\ncode, and the shape of the program lives only in your head. SoraMech makes\nthe shape visible and editable. The map file IS the program. If you can\nread JSON, you can read the program. If you can draw boxes, you can change\nit.\n\nThe second reason is language agnosticism. A box can call a Lua function,\na C function, a bash script, or a program written in anything the user\ndefines a driver for. The engine doesn't care. It invokes a driver, gets\noutputs, threads them to the next box. The map author picks the language;\nthe engine picks up the result.\n\nComponents\n----------\n\nThree programs share one data format — the map directory:\n\n  soramech-server.lua   — thin HTTP file proxy. Receives edits from the\n                          browser, reads and writes map files on disk.\n                          Started when remote editing is desired. Ignorant\n                          of the runner.\n\n  soramech-runner.lua   — FSM execution engine. Reads a map directory,\n                          walks the graph, invokes language drivers,\n                          threads outputs through wires. Started by the\n                          user from the CLI, a cronjob, or any external\n                          trigger. Ignorant of the server. Writes output\n                          to map-defined locations (data files, /tmp/).\n\n  index.html            — browser editor. Infinite-canvas box diagram.\n                          Reads and writes map files by talking to the\n                          server (local or remote). Never knows whether\n                          the runner is active.\n\nThe map directory is the stable interface. Server and runner share nothing\nbut the files.\n\nMap file layout\n---------------\n\nEach map lives in its own directory:\n\n  maps/<map-name>/\n    boxes/\n      <id>.json         — one file per box, self-contained, lists both\n                          incoming and outgoing connections\n    data/\n      <name>.json       — persistent data files (lua tables as JSON)\n                          sections are flagged constant: true or false\n    drivers.json        — language driver definitions (how to invoke each\n                          file extension)\n    meta.json           — map name, description, entry box id\n\n  tmp/                  — symlink to /tmp/<map-name>/\n                          holds ephemeral state: run logs, scratch tables,\n                          last-run snapshot\n\nBox file format\n---------------\n\nEach box is a JSON file in boxes/. It contains:\n\n  id          unique string identifier\n  label       human-readable name shown in the UI\n  kind        \"call\" | \"branch\" | \"data\"\n  ref         for \"call\": path like \"src/strings.lua\" or \"src/trim.sh\"\n  fn          for \"call\": function name (omitted for binary/shell refs)\n  inputs      list of {name, type} — what the box expects\n  outputs     list of {name, type} — what the box returns (tuple order)\n  connections list of {from_output, to_box_id, to_input, predicate?}\n              — written to BOTH endpoint files; runner validates at load\n\nBranch boxes have named output ports instead of positional outputs. Each\nport carries an optional predicate (comparator + literal). An \"else\" port\nalways exists. For LLM-based classification, \"else\" retries upstream\n(user wires it); for numeric/string predicates, \"else\" must be explicitly\nhandled or the runner refuses to start the map.\n\nLanguage drivers\n----------------\n\ndrivers.json maps file extensions to shell commands. Example:\n\n  {\n    \".lua\":  \"drivers/lua-driver.sh\",\n    \".c\":    \"drivers/c-driver.sh\",\n    \".sh\":   \"drivers/bash-driver.sh\"\n  }\n\nEach driver script receives: file path, function name, arg count, args...\nIt returns outputs on stdout, one per line (or as JSON for structured\nvalues). Lua and C ship as pre-written driver scripts — no special cases\nin the engine. If the user wants Rust, they write a driver script.\n\nThe C driver checks whether the source has changed since the last compile\n(by comparing mtime of .c against mtime of cached binary). If changed, it\ncompiles before invoking. Cache lives in tmp/.\n\nState and output\n----------------\n\nPersistent data lives in maps/<map-name>/data/ as JSON files. Each file\nis a Lua table serialized with dkjson. A file-level or section-level\n\"constant\" flag marks read-only data.\n\nEphemeral state (run logs, scratch variables, last-run snapshot) lives in\ntmp/ which is a symlink to /tmp/<map-name>/. It is fast, in RAM, and\nintentionally discarded on reboot.\n\nExecution model (v1)\n--------------------\n\nThe runner is synchronous in v1. Each box invocation is wrapped in a\ntask_fn(inputs) -> outputs boundary — the same signature as the 3d-rts\nthread pool's action chain — so the transition to concurrent execution is\na runtime swap, not a rewrite.\n\neffil-jit is available for threading when the custom thread pool (from\nthe 3d-rts project) is ready to be integrated. The target model is:\nboxes whose inputs are all satisfied fire concurrently; boxes that depend\non a still-running box park until that result arrives.\n\nMultiple maps can run concurrently as separate runner processes. Each map\nis a cohesive program. Maps calling into other maps is a future feature;\nfor now they are separate.\n\nFuture directions\n-----------------\n\n  — Integration with SoraMind: boxes that call inference endpoints on the\n    Alpine cluster, routing results through the map graph.\n\n  — Concurrent execution via the custom thread pool from 3d-rts,\n    replacing the synchronous v1 runner.\n\n  — Map-to-map calls: a box that invokes another map as a subroutine,\n    passing values across the boundary.\n\n  — Remote runner: a runner process on the Alpine cluster, controlled by\n    the web editor from another machine, results written to shared storage.\n\n  — Visual run trace: replay a completed run in the browser, seeing which\n    boxes fired and what values flowed through each wire.\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/notes/vision"
        }
      }],

          "content":"# SoraMech — Table of Contents\n\nRead in order for a complete picture of the system.\n\n## Notes\n\n- [notes/vision](../notes/vision) — what this is and why it has this shape\n\n## Documentation\n\n- [docs/001-architecture.md](001-architecture.md) — components, data flow, file format spec\n- [docs/002-roadmap.md](002-roadmap.md) — phases, goals, and sequencing\n- [docs/003-driver-system.md](003-driver-system.md) — language driver interface spec\n\n## Source\n\n- src/ — server, runner, and shared utilities (populated as issues complete)\n\n## Issues\n\n- [issues/phase-1-progress.md](../issues/phase-1-progress.md) — phase 1 status\n\n### Phase 1 — Foundation\n\n- 101 — project scaffold and map directory format\n- 102 — language driver interface\n- 103 — runner: graph loader and validator\n- 104 — runner: synchronous executor (task boundary)\n- 105 — HTTP server: file CRUD API\n- 106 — web editor: canvas and box rendering\n- 107 — web editor: wiring and connection UI\n- 108 — branch box and predicate routing\n- 109 — data files: persistent and ephemeral storage\n- 110 — phase 1 demo\n\n### Phase 2 — Concurrent execution\n\n- TBD after phase 1 completes\n\n### Phase 3 — SoraMind integration\n\n- TBD\n\n## Libraries\n\n- libs/ — vendored libraries (dkjson, luasocket)\n",

```json
{
  "isSidechain":false,
  "timestamp":"2026-05-07T22:25:35.471Z",
  "gitBranch":"HEAD",
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "sessionId":"2029ad16-5678-4b15-931f-3f52d826597a",
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "name":"Write",

          "type":"direct"
        },
        "input":{
          "content":"# SoraMech — Architecture\n\n## Three programs, one data format\n\nSoraMech is three independent programs that share a common on-disk format:\nthe map directory. None of the three knows about the others at runtime.\n\n```\n  Browser (index.html)\n       |  HTTP (file CRUD)\n       v\n  soramech-server.lua          [map directory]\n                               maps/<name>/\n                                 boxes/\n                                 data/\n                                 drivers.json\n                                 meta.json\n                                 tmp/ -> /tmp/<name>/\n       ^\n       | reads & writes\n  soramech-runner.lua\n```\n\n### soramech-server.lua\n\nThin HTTP proxy. Receives JSON requests from the browser and translates\nthem into file reads and writes on the map directory. No logic beyond\npath validation and basic consistency checks (e.g., reject a delete if\nthe box is still referenced by another box's connection list).\n\nStarted with: `luajit soramech-server.lua <maps-root> [port]`\nDefault port: 7700\n\nEndpoints (all operate on map files):\n  GET  /maps                        list maps\n  GET  /maps/<name>/boxes           list box IDs\n  GET  /maps/<name>/boxes/<id>      read box file\n  PUT  /maps/<name>/boxes/<id>      write box file\n  DELETE /maps/<name>/boxes/<id>    remove box (validates no dangling refs)\n  GET  /maps/<name>/data/<name>     read data file\n  PUT  /maps/<name>/data/<name>     write data file\n  GET  /maps/<name>/drivers         read drivers.json\n  PUT  /maps/<name>/drivers         write drivers.json\n  GET  /maps/<name>/meta            read meta.json\n\n### soramech-runner.lua\n\nFSM execution engine. Loads a map directory, validates the graph, then\nexecutes boxes in dependency order. Each box invocation is wrapped in a\n`task_fn(inputs) -> outputs` call — matching the 3d-rts thread pool's\naction chain signature for future threading compatibility.\n\nStarted with: `luajit soramech-runner.lua <map-dir>`\n\nExecution steps:\n  1. Read all box files from boxes/\n  2. Validate: all connection endpoints exist, branch \"else\" handled\n  3. Determine entry box from meta.json\n  4. Execute: resolve inputs, invoke driver, collect outputs, fire wires\n  5. On completion, write last-run snapshot to tmp/last-run.json\n\n### index.html\n\nStatic HTML + vanilla JS. Infinite-scroll canvas. Box diagram editor.\nTalks to soramech-server.lua for all file operations. No run button —\nthe user starts the runner separately from the terminal.\n\n## Map directory format\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/\n  meta.json          — { name, description, entry_box_id }\n  drivers.json       — { \".lua\": \"drivers/lua.sh\", \".c\": \"drivers/c.sh\", ... }\n  boxes/\n    <id>.json        — one file per box (see Box file format below)\n  data/\n    <name>.json      — lua table as JSON; sections have \"constant\": bool\n  drivers/\n    lua.sh           — built-in lua driver (shipped with soramech)\n    c.sh             — built-in C driver\n    bash.sh          — built-in bash driver\n  tmp/               — symlink to /tmp/<name>/\n    last-run.json    — snapshot of last run (ephemeral)\n    logs/            — run logs\n    cache/           — compiled binaries (C driver cache)\n```\n\n## Box file format\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"unique-string\",\n  \"label\": \"Human name\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"ref\": \"src/strings.lua\",\n  \"fn\": \"trim\",\n  \"inputs\": [\n    { \"name\": \"text\", \"type\": \"string\" }\n  ],\n  \"outputs\": [\n    { \"name\": \"result\", \"type\": \"string\" }\n  ],\n  \"connections\": [\n    {\n      \"from_output\": \"result\",\n      \"to_box\": \"next-box-id\",\n      \"to_input\": \"text\"\n    }\n  ],\n  \"ui\": { \"x\": 120, \"y\": 340 }\n}\n```\n\nFor branch boxes (`\"kind\": \"branch\"`):\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"classify\",\n  \"kind\": \"branch\",\n  \"inputs\": [{ \"name\": \"value\", \"type\": \"string\" }],\n  \"ports\": [\n    { \"name\": \"rogue\", \"predicate\": { \"op\": \"eq\", \"value\": \"rogue\" } },\n    { \"name\": \"wizard\", \"predicate\": { \"op\": \"eq\", \"value\": \"wizard\" } },\n    { \"name\": \"else\" }\n  ],\n  \"connections\": [...]\n}\n```\n\nConnections are written to BOTH endpoint box files. The runner validates\nat load time that both ends agree. Disagreement is a hard error.\n\n## Language driver interface\n\nDrivers are shell scripts. The engine invokes them as:\n\n  <driver-script> <file-path> <fn-name> <arg-count> [<arg1> <arg2> ...]\n\nOutputs are returned as JSON on stdout. Exit code non-zero = box failure.\nSee docs/003-driver-system.md for the full driver contract.\n\n## Execution model (v1 — synchronous)\n\nThe runner walks the graph depth-first from the entry box. Each box call:\n\n  1. Collect inputs: read wired output values from predecessor boxes\n  2. Invoke driver: shell out to the appropriate driver script\n  3. Collect outputs: parse JSON from driver stdout\n  4. Store outputs: held in runner memory, keyed by box id + output name\n  5. Fire connections: enqueue boxes whose input dependencies are now met\n\nEach step is wrapped in a `task_fn` boundary so the runner can be\nthreaded later by substituting the synchronous executor with one backed\nby effil-jit or the custom thread pool from the 3d-rts project.\n\n## Data files\n\nPersistent data lives in data/<name>.json. Format:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"constant\": false,\n  \"fields\": {\n    \"history\": [],\n    \"config\": { \"constant\": true, \"value\": { \"model\": \"soramind-default\" } }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nTop-level `constant: true` makes the whole file read-only. Individual\nfields can be flagged constant within an otherwise mutable file.\n\nEphemeral state (scratch tables, logs, last-run snapshot) goes to tmp/,\nwhich is a symlink to /tmp/<map-name>/. It survives the run but not a\nreboot — intentionally.\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/001-architecture.md"
        }
      }],

## [115]

```json
{
  "isSidechain":false,
